node.label: Lawrence Stone
node.date_label: The Crisis of the Aristocracy (1965) · The Family, Sex and Marriage in England (1977) · The Family, Sex and Marriage: abridged edition (1979) · “The Revival of Narrative” (1979)
node.description: A historian of early modern England whose studies of social structure and family relations also generated methodological disputes. The selected 1979 abridgment of his family study qualifies change by social strata, reversals and overlapping household types, while making a disputed assumption about surviving personal documents. His 1979 narrative essay identifies a shift among a prominent minority, rather than announcing that quantitative history had ended. Pollock’s source criticism and Hobsbawm’s response remain substantive qualifications to those arguments.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Crisis of the Aristocracy (1965); The Family, Sex and Marriage in England, 1500–1800 (1977; abridged 1979); “The Revival of Narrative” (1979).
node.scope_note: Existing lawrence_stone reused. The selected primary abridgment is not conflated with the 1977 text. Pollock’s 1981 thesis remains separate from the 1983 book. Prior source notes and the distinct Tuchman exchange remain untouched; no blanket anti-quantitative position or whole-book reading.

proposed_edges.relationship: Offers a qualified interpretation of family change and affective relations whose evidential assumptions Pollock disputes.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary abridgment pp. 21–29 and Pollock’s separate 1981 thesis passages, within existing scopes. Stone acknowledges literate-source bias while assuming broad representativeness; neither his trajectory nor that assumption is certified.

proposed_edges.relationship: Diagnoses renewed narrative among a prominent minority while acknowledging continuing quantitative and analytical work.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Existing primary Stone reading covers pp. 3–6 and 13–24, not 7–12; Hobsbawm response read completely. Diagnosis and examples remain Stone’s situated claims, not a unanimous field transition.
